passages.t: ‘Send out Your light and Your truth’: the end of the poem
passages.happening:
Psalm 43 has no heading. It goes straight on from Psalm 42. “Vindicate me, O God, and plead my case against an ungodly nation; deliver me from deceitful and unjust men” (verse 1).

He still does not understand. “For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me?” (verse 2). The second question is almost word for word the one in Psalm 42:9.

Then something new comes in. For the first time he asks God to bring him home. “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain, and to the place where You dwell” (verse 3). He pictures himself back there. “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (verse 4).

The poem closes with the refrain a third time: “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Psalms 42 and 43 are one poem in two psalms. Psalm 43 has no heading of its own, which is rare in Book Two. The same refrain runs through both (42:5, 42:11 and 43:5), and some Hebrew copies from the Middle Ages write them as one psalm. Most readers now take them together, as three stanzas. The note on Psalm 42 gives the heading and the setting.

‘Vindicate me’ and ‘plead my case’ are words from a law court. He asks God to be both his lawyer and his judge against people who have lied about him. That is not a claim to be sinless. The book page explains this kind of prayer under ‘When a psalmist says he is innocent’.

‘Your holy mountain’ is Zion, where the temple stood. ‘The harp’ is the lyre, the common stringed instrument of worship. In his mind he is already back among the temple singers.
passages.later:
Light and truth are sent out like two guides to walk him home. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6).

The psalmist longs for the altar. The letter to the Hebrews says that through Jesus believers now “have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place” (Hebrews 10:19), and calls them to “draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:22).
passages.asks:
The refrain is the same in all three places, but the stanza before it has changed. In Psalm 42 he looked back at what he had lost. Here he looks forward and asks to be led. Nothing outside has changed yet. What has changed is the direction he is facing.

If you have read Psalm 42 and stopped, read this one too. The poem is not finished until here. And notice the name he gives God in verse 4: ‘my greatest joy’. He is still far away when he says it.
